speaker: Phil Hufford
words: There are ways to determine the source of plutonium, whether it comes from the plant or whether it is indeed a product of atmospheric testing. Can you tell us a little bit about how those distinctions can be made?

speaker: Paula Elofson-Gardine
words: A little bit, yes. This is something that we have found to be true across the board with the production facilities that they all have a unique role to play with different isotopes, and these are like markers of where this has come from what it, what it's doing out there. The Rocky Flats plant receives waste from all over the country for reprocessing, recycling, and that was their argument with the large tritium scare in Broomfield years ago, that they had some tritium contaminated scrap or something, and that that's where it came from, and that the isotope matched that of Savannah, or wherever it was from at the time, that that was the origin of that. Well, it still doesn't excuse what they're doing out there. The fact is, it's coming from the plant. We don't have much in terms of above ground testing at this point in time, and I just think that's pretty thin argument to keep saying that it's all background.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: Explain a little about that tritium release for our listeners.

speaker: Paula Elofson-Gardine
words: The city of Broomfield realized there was very large tritium problem in their reservoir that they were trying to identify where is this coming from, because the monthly monitoring reports from Rockwell said no, it's not coming from us. Well, who the heck else is it going to come from? They sampled closer and closer and closer up the creek until they got right to the release ducts, Rocky Flats, and of course there was some there, and only when they tested above the plant and below the plant from these water sources did they finally admit that, well, yeah, maybe it did come from us, which is a similar problem we have with reports and other items, where it's been their own reports, and we've said, what about this information? What do you have to say about it? Is this your signature on this report? And they look at, and they go, "Well, maybe. Well, gee, I just don't know where you're getting your information. I don't understand what your question is. And so let's go on to the next question."

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: What happened to the residents of Broomfield when the tritium was released into the Great Western Reservoir?

speaker: Paula Elofson-Gardine
words: Nothing, they took more samples, uh urine samples from the residents. Dr. Carl Johnson did do a report on this of the contamination of the municipal water supplies, and they found that the residents did have very elevated tritium in their urine.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: But there was no alternative water supply made available to the city of Broomfield?

speaker: Paula Elofson-Gardine
words: Yes, on a pretty routine basis, Broomfield commingles their water with Denver, and so this does help the situation somewhat.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: As I recall, that tritium release took place in 1973, so was the mixing of water taking place in 1973 so that it was diluted?

speaker: Paula Elofson-Gardine
words: That's something I'm not sure of. I'd have to go back and look at the reports.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: Are there monitors on the plant site itself? Is the Department of Energy monitoring releases at Rocky Flats nuclear weapons plant?

speaker: Paula Elofson-Gardine
words: Well, for what it's worth, yes, they do. My firm belief, and that of many others, is that it is an absolutely worthless monitoring program. What they pick up much of the time is resuspension. The emissions we firmly believe do not reach those monitors, so what you see is probably what their monthly resuspension looks like, if that was the dispersed form of plutonium that passes through the filters anyway, so I don't see that the monitoring program does any good.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: Is the state of Colorado monitoring emissions out there in an effective way?

speaker: Paula Elofson-Gardine
words: No, I don't believe they are.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: Have there been soil samples taken in Greeley or Fort Collins or some of these areas that might be liable to these high level winds carrying these micro plutonium particles?

speaker: Paula Elofson-Gardine
words: Yes, I understand that they have had a sampling program around the state. Their soil specialist travels all over the state different times, and I understand that part of that program is to try to establish quote background unquote. My feeling is that they are interested in knowing exactly where it's going to, but I don't know if we'll ever really see the truth of that. Brings to mind a study that they did, called Plutonium Burdens, and people living around Rocky Flats. They autopsied 519 people, some of them as far away as Lamar, Colorado, some in Sterling, and less than 10 people in that entire autopsy study came from within 10 kilometers of the plant, and to me they did find weapons-grade plutonium in people as far away as Lamar. Okay, but to me, what is significant about that study is that they almost completely bypassed the surrounding communities for that autopsy study, and I question the credibility of a study like that, where they fail to really look at the surrounding communities, and this ties into the unfortunate problems in the official foot dragging, and seeing that the appropriate epidemiology studies be done on surrounding communities.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: Now, I have seen maps that outline the extent of plutonium contamination based on some work done by a person named Cray and another person named Hardy. There's the Hardy Cray contours. These are map contours called isoplus, and they, they seem to indicate that the extent of the contamination really is towards the Denver area and not towards Boulder, and not to the west, or not far west of the plant, could you comment on the the accuracy or your sense of how valid those plutonium contamination contours are?

speaker: Paula Elofson-Gardine
words: Well, I, I feel that there is some controversy about that. The Crane Hardy report does indicate the wind roses, that is maps of the wind patterns during the two major incidents, 57 and 69 One of them went almost directly south to Leyden, and the other areas directly around Arvada. One of the other fires went primarily southeast in a direct line to Arvada, and then to Westminster as well. So the Crane Hardy map very curiously doesn't seem to cover those particular areas. So I wonder, where they're sampling, why didn't they sample in those areas that the wind roses seem to be pointing to for those serious incidents.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: How about Boulder or place, you know, Coal Creek Canyon? Do you think there's any contamination from the plant going northward?

speaker: Paula Elofson-Gardine
words: I'd like to refer that to Susan Hurst, the executive director for Networking Colorado.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: Tell us a little bit more about this land dispute, the Church McKay land, and what the issue was there, and where that land is, maybe how it relates to the Jefferson Center proposal, and the nature of the contamination that exists there.

speaker: Paula Elofson-Gardine
words: That's a very interesting question. The farmers in the area wasn't just Church McKay, there were others involved with this suit. They were suing, I believe, more on the concept of loss of property value because the contamination, which is an interesting point, because right now the rest of the communities are looking at this as a very serious issue, that a lot of people have the houses up for sale in countryside, Broomfield, Westminster, and they can't sell them, so I believe that this is an excellent basis for a current federal lawsuit. The farmers did receive a very lucrative out-of-court settlement, and here they are trying to make money on it again. I think it's just absolutely incredible that they want to have a giant development there, where the worst contamination spots were south, southeast, and east of the plant. They want to put W470 through that and have that vehicular traffic add to the resuspension problems. By developing, they will kick up more of the contamination. They have right across that south border, where they have a lot of those landowners that already receive settlement participating and wanting to sell this to the City of Arvada, or to whatever company wants to help with the development. I cannot imagine someone in their right mind wanting to be part of that development, or to have an office out there where their air conditioning system would be taking in available radionuclides and poisoning their employees as they work. I think that it's criminally negligent that they would do this. The emergency preparedness director, Jeff Everett, has told us when we had lunch with him during the WIPP hearings, the waste isolation pilot plant, that the emergency preparedness people are not ready for a drastic emergency out there, such as the 57 fire, when people should have been evacuated and were not. That should we have nifty little 7/11 stores out there? I'd hope that they'd make them like bomb shelters, because the emergency preparedness team would not go within the four mile radius, so I'd like to know how long they would expect people to remain in those 7/11 stores eating nachos and hot dogs, because they certainly would not be allowed to go out, and they would not be evacuated by anyone else. And according to Jeff Everett, people would be told when it was okay to go out after the plume had passed, and they had sampled to see if it was okay to go out yet.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: Can you speak to this question of criticalities at the plant? I know this topic was brought up to the governor. Can you explain what a criticality is, and whether any have happened out there, and what the implications of that are?

speaker: Paula Elofson-Gardine
words: There's a lot of controversy about this particular issue as well. We understand from the environmental impact statement that solution criticality is a large problem out there, and that the janitors have holes in their buckets, so they don't have too much water to get in with their plutonium particles, they may pick up on their mops. That what happens when plutonium comes into contact with air is spontaneous combustion. Okay, if plutonium comes into contact with water, you have fission. Now there was like 40,000 gallons plus of water that they tried to put out a plutonium fire with in 1957. They believe that this is where a lot of the cesium came from out there, and strontium there is cesium and strontium out there in the soils around the plant, around the 903 pad area. It's in that report that they have found it out there. It's not from background, it's not from anywhere else. It is from Rocky Flats.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: What report?

speaker: Paula Elofson-Gardine
words: There's a remedial investigation report on the 903 Padmound and East Trenches areas that Rockwell provided to the EPA, so they can't say that they're unaware of it or that it's a load of malarkey. It's there, Dr. Johnson found detectable limits of this way back when he did his first soil study. So, this is why it alarmed him, so that he tried to make the public aware of it.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: Explain what a criticality is.

speaker: Paula Elofson-Gardine
words: A criticality is like a burst of neutrons.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: Is it a chain reaction, or what is it?

speaker: Paula Elofson-Gardine
words: I would say similar to that. I probably should, probably should have you clip that part and look it up for you real quick. Okay, when a criticality occurs, it can be very, it can be a very small thing, and it can be very big thing. I think what a lot of people think of when they think of criticality is critical mass and chain reaction. That's something that I believe they came very close to 1957 because of the enormity of what was released, and the water involved with it, and the whole thing. Criticality is the state where fission starts, and you have a release of energy, and it tends to be energy that goes through people gets into everything, that's where they say something is radioactively hot.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: We're talking about release of neutrons?

speaker: Paula Elofson-Gardine
words: Right, release of neutrons. Its that blue flash when they show like dark circle and they show them milling this stuff, you see little blue flashes here and there, those are release of neutrons. Okay, so it's a reaction that occurs very naturally with plutonium that they would like to keep to a minimum, because of the great risk to the workers and to the people around that you have these energy releases going out.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: I know that Dr. Carl Johnson, in describing the fire, quote unquote fire, that happened in 1957 speculated that it was a fission reaction that blew out 600 of these HEPA filters, what do you think?

speaker: Paula Elofson-Gardine
words: I think that he's absolutely right on the money. I think with the problems that Jim Stone, the engineer that used to be at the plant, has described in terms of plutonium sand dunes and the air ducts and big gaps in the glove boxes, those glove boxes are supposed to be kept in a negative environment, negative atmosphere environment, which means they like pump in nitrogen and things like that, and when it's exposed to oxygen, you have this combustion happening, and if it gets too far out of control, then you have fissioning happening, and this is the critical thing, criticality. And the fact that it got so far out of control that they had this huge blowout, and then continuous problem, they had an area without criticality drains that they were pumping all this water into, trying to put it out. They didn't know what the heck they were doing.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: So by pumping the water in there, they were just making the situation worse.

speaker: Paula Elofson-Gardine
words: That's where you get into the fissioning situation, where most people typically think of the China syndrome and meltdown, and it's a very serious problem, needless to say. That they put the worst thing on it they possibly could have, and I think that's where they had, they probably added to the fire rather than help put it out at that particular point.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: What measures should people take if they find themselves passing by the plant, or if they, you know, if they're forced to go out there for some reason, or is there any reason for people to be concerned about driving by the Rocky Flats plant?

speaker: Paula Elofson-Gardine
words: Well, I'll put it this way, Sue and I have had friends tell us that she had a scientist friend whose wife got a flat tire out there on the east side, and he went out to help her, and he had his trunk full of sophisticated equipment for measuring this kind of stuff, and it started going off like crazy. It scared the heck out of them, and they wanted to get out of there. They didn't even want to take the car. I think that this is a public health threat that certainly is available to the public, and I think if you can avoid at least going around the east side of the plant, don't drive down that road. People shouldn't be there. It's ridiculous. We keep our windows up when we go around the plant, because we don't want to have that coming into the car.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: What advice would you give to people who might be thinking of participating in the, in the proposed encirclement of Rocky Flats on August 6th.

speaker: Paula Elofson-Gardine
words: I think that they should be getting a very good insurance policy, and I would hold Colorado Freeze Boulder criminally liable for any radiation-induced cancers from partaking in that event. I think it's criminally negligent for them, knowing what we know now that they did not know before, to go ahead with this kind of an activity that is so opportunist.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: Okay. all right, we're almost out of time here. Any anything else you'd like to bring up?

speaker: Paula Elofson-Gardine
words: I want the public to be aware that just because the FBI came and went doesn't mean that the situation is over. We have had a crisis situation here, it's been very hard to get people to listen to what's going on, and to take a look at the facts. Thank God, the FBI took it seriously, and they felt that they had enough proof to go in there. I think that the public needs to be aware that the problem has not gone away. This place should never have been built as close to a community. We've got to close it, and we've got to start the cleanup, and there will be continual problems out there until it is resolved, and the public has a right to know, and they have a right to be alarmed about it, and they have the right to demand to the governor, to the legislators, and to Washington to help us to eradicate this problem here.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: All right. Thank you, Paula. We've been speaking with Paula Elofson Gardine, who is Director of Health Technicians for a Cleaner Colorado. I'm sorry, Concerned Health Technicians for a Cleaner Colorado, and an acknowledged expert on some of the health aspects of the Rocky Flats nuclear weapons plant. Thank you, Paula.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: Okay, a clarification here. Paula Elofson Gardine is a citizen expert on the extent of the contamination from the Rocky Flats nuclear weapons plant and the pathways of exposure to that contamination.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: Today is July 5th 1989, and we have with us Susan Hurst. Do you prefer to Susan or Sue, Sue, we have Sue Hurst with us, who is director of Networking Colorado and is a citizen expert in the contaminate in the area of the contamination from Rocky Flats nuclear weapons plant, as well as the channels of exposure to that contamination, and she also is project coordinator for Sierra Club, and what project is that? The Rocky Flats project coordinator for the Sierra Club. Let's start with some of the questions of contamination. Can you help our listeners understand the patterns of contamination of the windborne or airborne contaminants from Rocky Flats. What, what pattern of exposures the public getting?

speaker: Sue Hurst
words: Well, there's a misconception about downwinders, because in our area of the state we have the flat irons on the west side of the plant, and then you've got the planes on the east side of the plant with our water reservoirs directly east and therefore when they cited Rocky Flats with all their geological surveys and everything in their own Rockwell's report stated that the wind patterns go from the east to the west and from south to north and that is exactly the opposite of how the winds go, and frequently in the spring and the fall we have Chinook winds that go from the west to the east, frequently 90 to 120 miles an hour, and in Rockwell's reports, or Dow Chemical at the time, Department of Energy reports, they stated that the winds rarely went over 30 miles an hour, and that's just not true in this part of the country. Also, with the canyons directly west of the plant, in the evening, as the ground cools, you will have the canyons sucking the air, if you will, up the canyons. As the air warms up again, it comes down the canyon. So, with these radioactive emissions, you have the canyons sucking it up in the mornings as it's cool, and then as it heats up during the day, it comes back down. So, the canyons get the double whammy effect. Also, frequently in the mornings, the wind will go over Boulder, and again, as it heats up, it comes back down around, as you can see, with the brown cloud. The brown cloud will travel around Denver area, it will go out over Greeley and Fort Collins, pick up more particulates from the stockyards and things, and then come back over in the late afternoon, as we've seen many, many times, and we'll have the wind, the air inversions trapping these particulates over the Denver area, so it's, it's dispersing constantly, and it does not stay in one place, and that's something particular to our area. If you'll see turn of the century pictures, you will see the brown cloud hanging over Denver with horse and carriages, so new travel modes of travel does not really affect what happened at the turn of the century, it's the same, we're in a dust bowl area right here, and it goes around in a clockwise pattern daily, so you've got this heavy concentration of radioactivity clinging to our air particulates at our high altitude with our thin, thin atmosphere here.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: Are we talking primarily about plutonium, or are there other, other radioactive substances?

speaker: Sue Hurst
words: Well, there's a lot more to be worried about than plutonium. Plutonium, of course, is something to be very concerned about, but we also have americium, which is more radioactive than plutonium. We also have, when they burn agent orange, you get dioxin. We believe that they were burning agent orange last summer, because we have found, and I believe the FBI will conclude with what I believe that we have got dioxin in the area, as well as arsenic. We've got quite a number of things that are very bad for any living being, and uranium also. And I'm not talking background uranium, I'm talking weapons grade uranium.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: Can you tell our listeners something about the daily emissions coming from that plant? Most people feel that there were a couple of major releases in a fire 1957 and a fire 1969. What is the nature of the releases of toxic radioactive and other materials from that plant?

speaker: Sue Hurst
words: Quite honestly, it's mind-boggling how much they do out there. We had the big issue of their fluidized bed incinerator, which was a fiasco, to say the least. They had one incident where the incinerator got out of control and it melted a viewing room window before they could get to it and correct the feed going into it. That seemed to pass by the public that they were not going to utilize this fluidized bed incinerator, but the fact of the matter is they've got incinerators going every day out there, burning radioactive waste to recover plutonium, and we've got 50 vents pumping this out every day around the clock, whether we have air inversions or not. So, so basically, you've got people that cannot burn fireplaces on air inversion days, but they can burn radioactive material out at Rocky Flats, which I don't feel is right. So, we've got a smelting plant here in the Denver metro area that is pumping this out. They also have, they refer, Rocky Flats refers to reverse osmosis system, which should clean their wastewater before it's put in their settling ponds, and they have a series of ponds, A, B, and C series. They do not use the reverse osmosis plant because they are not set up to handle the waste that this reverse osmosis would produce, so they are not cleaning out the heavy metals or radioactivity from the water, if they do not release these ponds into the reservoirs, they spray irrigate this onto 600 some odd acres, and so you've got radioactive and toxic waste in the spray irrigation areas, and this, of course, is groundwater runoff, and their argument that it's all within background levels of whatever exotic thing you would like to come up with, it's within background levels, and believe me, there are no background levels in this area for weapons grade uranium, plutonium, americium, cesium, and I could go on and on. The other things they had, and it's, it's funny if you look at it in the context of some farmer out in the middle of Texas with his own little private dump, which you know a lot of people do back there, and they were just, if you will, out the back door dumping their chemicals and having open pit uranium burning with their depleted uranium chips, which is more radioactive than when they started with it. So they've got many, many, many areas that are of vital concern now. You've got the solar evaporation ponds, which is a concentrating mechanism to dry up their sludge and then put it in star-shaped containers, and make pond crete out of it, which is like radioactive concrete. However, someone from construction needs to be in there and tell them how to mix it right, so it's not the consistency of mayonnaise. They need to make it harder and more stable, just to keep it from spreading to the community. You've got the 903 pad area, which they covered over with asphalt after they discovered barrels and barrels and barrels of contaminated, radioactively contaminated lathe oil that was leaking into the dirt, and the dirt was then suspended by the wind for years and years and years, and they covered it over with asphalt, and believe me, what's coming out over the top of that asphalt is radioactivity. If you think of a banana peel that's been sitting in the sun for a week and the fruit flies over it, that radioactivity is not going to be staying over the banana peel when the wind goes over, it's going to be spreading it, and it will to the community, and I believe that this form of dispersion is what has settled on the top of our reservoirs. Now the city of Westminster has a surface water skimmer, so they skim the top of the surface. Which one is it?

speaker: Sue Hurst
words: Well, there's one city that has. A surface skimmer that will skim the top for the water for the cities, and this is not that secure feeling for me to think of getting the top part of the lake, however, you got the bottom part too of where the sediment is, and twice a year we've got lake turnover, so the lake is trying to clean itself, and in the process, it's resuspending all this radioactive and toxic chemicals, and we will have elevated readings during this period of time when we have the lake turnover, so we need to have some remediation done in that area. And speaking of remediation, when we do start having the cleanup, we need to have a very close eye done on this, because in the past we've had practices such as trying to plow under two inches plutonium, and then put more topsoil on top of that, but what we found is that during the plowing, if you come from South Dakota, Iowa, Nebraska, you understand how the dust goes everywhere, and again we have elevated readings of radioactivity in all the air monitors around the area in Arvada, Westminster, and you have the erosion. They have put soil sterilant out there in many areas, not too, so that they can remediate in this particular way by sterilizing the soil. I'm not sure what they had in mind, but they're having a hard time finding ground cover now, and so you've got constant erosion, constant wind patterns. I mean, Colorado is extremely windy, as we all know that live here, and this is directly, it just blows right to us. So, plowing is not acceptable, but it was the cheapest method, and so that is what they used. Now, the Jefferson County Board of Health is the branch that issued a dust permit, a fugitive dust permit, and Gary Potter from Rockwell was sitting on the Jefferson County board. He thereafter, after they gave the fugitive dust permit, he resigned, saying that it could be misconstrued as a conflict of interest, since he was more than willing to give his expertise in this area up until they got their permit, and then he quit. Of course, it was inappropriate. We all knew that, and now we've got a main problem with how we're going to do the remediation, how we can keep our finger on top of these committees, governmental branches, so that we don't get exposed to even more emissions from the plant, whether it's from the venting of it from their smelting operations or if it's from the plowing, I believe that we need to have containment domes built before they dig into the 881 hillside area, but then you've got to think about the workers that are going to be going into the containment domes, it's going to be highly concentrated and I think I've got a plan that may be workable. I think we've got an awful lot of people that might disagree with me, but I think we need to take people from death row and put them out there in those containment domes to start doing cleanup, and that might be a deterrent against crime.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: What would you say the level, excuse me, what would you say the level of daily emissions is out there? Are we talking about very, very minor, difficult to measure amounts, or are we talking about something more substantial?

speaker: Sue Hurst
words: Well, with the monitoring devices we've got out there right now, that they're only four feet up off the ground, and they're picking up an awful lot of resuspended dust. What we need is to have these monitors put at the top of the poles, 10 to 20 feet high, and we need more than a vacuum pump system. We need more of the state of the art monitoring equipment. We need to have monitoring equipment in the stacks to see what's coming out of the stack, not what's showing up at the perimeter of the fence line, and they also need to put in monitors that will pick up everything, not just radioactive things, but all the toxics that come out as well when they're doing their chemical recovery process, so right now we don't know. I do know that they have criticalities all the time. They have their own fire department, and anybody that's got a CB radio can pick up their own particular radio band and hear how many times a fire department is called out to different buildings for criticality fires.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: Are these criticality fires in any way explosions?

speaker: Sue Hurst
words: There's a difference between... What a lot of people don't understand is that we won't have a giant explosion, we'll have the biggest unquenchable fire in the world. It'll make Chernobyl look very small, because we've got a plutonium vault out at Rocky Flats that has probably tons of plutonium that has to be in a special cooled area that is, if they would have a power outage, if their generator wouldn't kick on, that stuff would heat up, and believe me, this place would be the dead zone. Nobody could live here, and it would go around the world, what would happen here. They could not put the fire out.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: Wow. How about leakage into the water supply, they have maintained that there is no substantial regular leakage of radionuclides or of other toxic substances into Woman Creek and Walnut Creek. What, what do you think about those claims?

speaker: Sue Hurst
words: They're lying, they're stretching the truth. I like to refer to the Water Act as the Dirty Convoluted Polluted Water Act, because what the health department and EPA has said is allowable is not allowable at all. Again, I refer to their reverse osmosis system. They do not have it. They do not utilize it. I don't even know if the plant's been completed yet, because they constantly referred to in the early 1980s our RO system will be up and ready to go, but it is not ready to go, and it is not usable. This may maintain that their holding ponds are settling ponds, and when the contaminants have settled to the bottom as much as they think they will, they will, if you will, skim off the top now. Frequently, you will see they have 30 to 50 million gallons released monthly. Where do they put it? It does not evaporate on site. They have to release it, and they quite often do release it. Otherwise, they wouldn't be keeping track of how much was going into these Great Western Reservoir and Stanley Lake, they are releasing it. It is contaminated, and if they don't do that, they spray irrigate this stuff, and that has to come in groundwater runoff. Now think about the saturation of the ground on those spray fields, that's got to be going into our groundwater runoff, and that in turn soaks down, down, down into the bedrock and down into our aquifers. I mean, it only makes sense.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: Do you think that the Environmental Protection Agency has first of all, does the Environmental Protection Agency have a role in monitoring what goes on at the Rocky Flats nuclear weapons plant?

speaker: Sue Hurst
words: They have a role, but I don't think they've taken a very active role, and I think their hands have been tied, which is verified through the memo that Mary Walker put out to Admiral Foley, stating that there they wanted to finesse the compliance agreement, which was the sweetheart deal between the state EPA and the Health Department of Colorado, that they wanted the language vague, so that nobody had any authorization or control over what's happening out at Rocky Flats, so you've got from the very top, top, top level, no control, no jurisdiction. We don't want anybody to have control, and above all, we don't want to look like we're welching on our own deals to make sure that the public is safe.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: So, when you said in the state EPA, are you talking about the state and the state being the Colorado Department of Health, and then the EPA?

speaker: Sue Hurst
words: Yes, jointly, and the Department of Energy also comes into this. Everybody comes into play here, and what I increasingly see is more evidence of the nuclear guinea pig theory. When they were taking these beagle dogs up in Fort Collins and exposing them to all sorts of radioactivity to see what it would do to their bodies, and then burning them up, or when in the 1940s was it? In that 30 years ago they were doing taking the elderly, prisoners, and children injecting them with thorium, was it strontium-92, plutonium, uranium, make... giving them injections, having them snort it to see what it would do to the body, to see how long it would take to have renal failure, to see what would  happen, they had some survivors, they had some that died immediately, hit them, and they were gone. But the thing is, our own government was doing this to us. When I read this report, my eyes about popped out of my head. I couldn't believe it was like it's like what they were doing to the people in Germany and Russia. Our own government, I'm not a communist, I'm very, very patriotic, and my father worked for Senator Armstrong, which is very right-wing man. But you see this kind of stuff, and you're going, "This isn't right. How can they do this, and how can people cover this up?" What they've done isn't right. Now, Alice Stewart, when she was in town talked about the healthy survivor effect. They look for very, very healthy workers to go to work out at Rockwell, so that it takes them longer to get any ill effects from what they've been doing. So it looks like everything is okey dokey out there, but healthy people in the population around as well, but there are some people, women and children, are more susceptible to this than men, and I think if we looked at the women and children in this area, we'd be awfully surprised and stunned at what has been happening to us.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: Tell me a little bit more about this study, where you heard about this testing on civilians and others by our own government. What study is that?

speaker: Sue Hurst
words: It is called... I get to the page here. It was a subcommittee for energy conservation and power. It's called the American Nuclear Guinea Pigs: three decades of radiation experiments on US citizens, and it was prepared by the Subcommittee on Energy Conservation and Power of the Committee on Energy and Commerce, US House of Representatives, November of 1986. Our own Senator Tim Worth sat on this committee, yet he still claims ignorance on what's going on here in Colorado. He was a part of the Lamm-Wirth report, and they stated close the plant, decommission it, but he still claims ignorance on what's going on. I believe that all of our politicians have well indeed known what's happening, the extent of it, how serious it is, and when we hear from the governor, there is no immediate health risk. What he's saying is number one, you've got to exposure, number two, you've got the latency period, don't worry about it right now, but you better worry in 20 years. So that, in that way, no, there is no immediate health risk. You're not, they keep saying we've got normal expected ranges of radioactivity for quote fallout from the nuclear testing, but from our viewpoint, number one, our state is the only state with a plutonium standard for the soil, and this was not done from a risk assessment, this was done from a sample on the east side of the plant to see number one, what was out there, and then they decided to build the standard around that.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: So they found what was there said, okay, this is the standard we'll use, because that's what's there now.

speaker: Sue Hurst
words: Correct. This also was set by an individual in the health department that was not qualified to do this kind of study, if you want to call it a study, and I see a lot of this covering of their own rear ends later on down the road, when they, when my own daughter, which was 11 years old at the time, had heard this particular person that set the standard talking with a Rockwell employee that was their soil analysis expert about how far down in the soil they were supposed to be going, "Was it five centimeters or eight centimeters? I don't remember which one is it that we're supposed to do." She came right back to me and told me their conversation, because those guys couldn't even remember what they're supposed to say. When you can't remember how you did your own analysis, that tells me that there's there's a problem. The problem is they can't remember because they're lying, or else they didn't do the studies.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: Explain a little bit more about how that level contamination level was set in Colorado.

speaker: Sue Hurst
words: The standard was set on what was found in the soil on the east side of the plant, and this was done not by risk assessment, but by what was already existing there. Doesn't mean it was safe, but it means that's what they set the standard at, because it was already there. Now, this same side of the plant was picking up in its own, in the monitors, the World Net Monitoring System, which picks up background fallout around the world. There's, I think, 32 stations around the world. The elevated readings was consistently thousands of times higher than any place else in the world. They disconnected this monitor because it was throwing off the statistics for the rest of the world, and it was picking up resuspended plutonium from road dust, from cars going by, if you will, and that tells me there's a problem over there on the east side of the plant because of this disconnection of the monitor system.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: How about the west, north, and south sides of the plant. What's the contamination like there?

speaker: Sue Hurst
words: Well, it's, it's high, but it's not as high, because you got the constant wind flow going from south to east. So, of course, it would concentrate on the southeast part of the plant. However, you still have the nighttime air that seems to pull towards the north, so in the evening you will have elevated readings on that side, now what they do is they take - they don't give you readings per day, although that's what I'd love to see when they have criticality fires out there, but what we see is a mixture of all their readings into one, so that anything high or elevated would be taken into a curve, if you will, so we don't see when there has been accidents. You only see, "My gosh, this month we've got awfully high readings of plutonium and uranium in the water." "What happened?" "Gee, we don't know. Nothing happened unusual."

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: Have there been any comparisons made of the soil and air levels of contaminants from Rocky Flats in Denver, as opposed to say Colorado Springs, or to Pueblo, or to Greeley, or you know, to cities far away from the plant.

speaker: Sue Hurst
words: Well, I know that I got a hold of some EPA documents that they do measure strontium-90 in the milk regularly all around the country, and I got a hold of a report that was done a month before Chernobyl happened, and then during Chernobyl you could see the waves of radiation in the cities it hit. Okay, and so they're monitoring it through the milk. They were also picking it up in the air and everything else, water, you name it. What I was seeing was elevated readings. The higher in altitude you go, so that part of the argument I somewhat believe you're higher in elevation, so naturally the air is thinner, and you will have higher concentrations of radioactivity in the air. However, Rocky Flats and Twin Falls, Idaho, are continually the highest readings you will ever see. Now, I've also discovered that after the Chernobyl accident, as the waves hit the different cities, elevated readings that lasted longer in the particular areas of this, of the country, where they have not just reactors but incinerators that incinerate radioactive material, Twin Falls, Idaho is one of them, so is Rocky Flats. Rocky Flats is always almost always the highest, we are higher here in radiation than at Ground Zero at Nevada. That tells me, I believe the industry used the Chernobyl accident to step up their production during the waves of radiation that were hitting the cities to mask their emissions.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: What once again, can you give our listeners some sense of the daily emission, the level of daily emissions? What I don't know how you would do that, but is there some way you can communicate? You said there are what, 50 vents or 50 vents through which there is some release of something. Is there some way to describe what that release is?

speaker: Sue Hurst
words: I would have to get out my monitoring reports and read you how many disintegrations per minute per gram there is compared with, say, Houston, Texas. I do know that reading all the different cities that they have listed, starting from Anchorage, Alaska to New Jersey, that you have to take very many things into consideration. Elevation is one of them, and industry is the other. What they have, and it's only by reading and looking at the figures yourself, which jumps out at your eyes first. We're the highest. I don't believe anybody would really understand. I know our state standard is two disintegrations per minute per soil gram of virgin undisturbed soil. Okay, so after the fire they had...

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: Which, which fire?

speaker: Sue Hurst
words: The 1957 fire, for some reason the monitors in the stacks were turned off for eight days. Okay, so after eight days they figured that they had 250 kilograms on the filters, okay, and the guidelines for these...

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: This is kilograms of plutonium?

speaker: Sue Hurst
words: Right, of plutonium. The emissions for eight days after the fire were exceeded 16,000 times for one day, in other words, the guidelines for a 50 year release were exceeded in one single day, or 13,000 microcuries of plutonium-239 on the eighth day after the fire in the explosion, which is kind of mind boggling. So then you think about the secret survey that the government did on what happened around the area, right? This is pretty incredible. Off-site contamination revealed at Ralston School, which is an elementary school, which is 12 miles south-southwest of the plant, showed 12,000 disintegrations per minute per kilogram of enriched uranium. At Semper Elementary school, six miles east of the plant, showed 16,000 disintegrations per minute per kilogram of enriched uranium. This is not background, this is enriched from this plant. They keep saying the elevated readings that we pick up in Denver is all background, because our area is so unique. Yeah, it's unique because we've got a nuclear weapons plant here, that's what makes it so unique. Now, at the Church property, the Church McKay land, where these people got $9 million in settlement, this is one of the reasons why. Church property showed 18,000 disintegrations per minute per kilogram of plutonium. These concentrations are 150, 200, and 225 times higher than plutonium concentrations in the soil from accumulated worldwide fallout from nuclear weapons testing the background levels in soil testing was 4,200 to 6,300 times higher than our background levels measured, say, from South Carolina. This tells me the health department knew everybody has known what's going on here. Why we keep having these people duck and cover, saying "we didn't know, we didn't know" is not a good way to deal with legislation issues that need to be passed now. I believe that we need to have the Department of Energy start funding our own hospitals with top-notch doctors and scientists to help us defray medical costs from effects from the fire, from the constant emissions, so that all of us don't have to go into the poorhouse trying to go to the doctor to get treatment from illnesses caused by emissions from this plant.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: Would you say that the Denver metropolitan area then is routinely being exposed to these emissions, and that say when it rains, that the rain washes out these particulates and washes them into the soil, or is there that sort of a mechanism working?

speaker: Sue Hurst
words: As a matter of fact, Dr. Harvey Nichols, a PhD from the University of Colorado, did an excellent report called Transactions of a Buffer Zone. He discovered plutonium, weapons-grade plutonium was in the snow crystals at Stanley Lake. This says to me that when the emissions are up in the air, the snow then comes down and scrubs the atmosphere, bringing the snow to the ground with the plutonium and all your other emissions in it, I mean, only makes sense. It's cleaning our atmosphere, just like we always thought, you know. It's like a miracle from God. He lets it rain and it's clean again. In our case, no, it's not clean again. It just raises our levels of plutonium, because only total complete snow cover will keep this radioactivity down, however, once it's done, an hour after it's done snowing, you have the bouncing up, if you will, of these little alpha particles, beta particles, and gamma. People should not be eating homegrown vegetables around the four mile area, because you will release plutonium particulates in the soil when you're even digging for flowers. The thing that got me was a report that I read. I couldn't believe it, because these people are so cold and ruthless about what they want. Children playing on dusty playgrounds will resuspend plutonium and inhale it. It through the dust that they're playing in, pets will get it on their fur, track it into the home, you will vacuum it up and resuspend the particles by vacuuming. You wash your dirty clothes when you're putting it through the dryer, the dryer vents it out again, and you're inhaling it again. It's so cold the way that they have done these reports, they know what it's doing, but they refuse to do anything to give us any relief from it. You think about what's in our water, the radioactivity in our water, and I'm not talking just background, I'm talking about what they're putting into it and what is going through our water treatment plants. The city of Aravada, Westminster, Boulder do not have reverse osmosis systems, so they cannot take this out of the water, and they don't. They have found that when you add chlorine to this particular kind of contamination, for instance, taking a shower is the worst way that you could probably inhale radioactivity, is through steam. It'll go right straight to the lungs, as well as drinking it. Chlorine helps assist the body in uptake of this stuff, so it's more insidious the more you try to remediate it, and I don't believe chlorinating it is remediation by any means.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: How about people living in central Denver or in Aurora, or should they not eat their vegetables?

speaker: Sue Hurst
words: I don't believe that the dispersion patterns have gone that severe in that part of the town. However, North Denver is... North Denver has shown on the isoplethic map from the Harding Cray report, and they are getting emissions. If we would do neighborhood checks, walk door to door, find out who lived where, for what time period, and start following up on the latency period, I think we'd find some alarming facts.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: How would you characterize the work of Dr. Carl Johnson in trying to determine the public health effects from the plant?

speaker: Sue Hurst
words: I think Dr. Johnson was brilliant. I think it took a lot of courage for him to come out and say what he felt was wrong, even though it cost him his career. He was a well-respected man around the world, everywhere except here in Colorado, by our own health department and politicians blackballed him until the day he died, and that man should be given a Nobel Peace Prize for what he has tried to do and tried to tell people what is happening out here. The fetal deaths that we got in this area after the 57 and 69 fire rose sharply, that was confirmed by the health department at what was last Tuesday, the 28th of June, when the governor was there, the 27th of June, 1989. The health department stated that in an area such as Rocky Flats, if there's an unacceptable or elevated radiation in the area, it will first show up in fetal deaths and miscarriages, and that just hit me in the heart when I heard that, that they know it does cause sterility too. It collects in the gonads, it collects in the ovary, the ovaries, and since Denver is number one in the nation for prostate cancer, I'm linking prostate cancer with the radioactive particles that Harvey Nichols study on snow crystals confirms. Radioactivity will cling to air particulates, we're number one in the nation for our brown cloud, we're number one for prostate cancer. This collects in the gonads. I wonder, our rates on cervical cancer, I mean, the two go hand in hand, if you will. We've got, I know, so many girls that have ovarian cysts and ovarian cancer. How much is going to be enough to stop what's going on. It's our kids and their kids. The sins are going to be visited from the Father to the children, you know. Just like in the Bible, I'm not, you know, a Bible freak, but some of this stuff, it does make you think what they're doing to us, and they don't care. Otherwise, they'd stop it. But the health department knows. I've got a friend that does oncology down in Denver, and he said he felt that since he'd seen so many cases from our area of people being treated for cancer, believe me, there's all sorts of kinds that come from this area that are unique to our area, he said there's so many girls at Pomona high school, coming down with breast cancer and breast tumors. He just said, "I'm wondering if on the north side of town we're seeing radiation sickness rather than the flu." Just gave me a chill down to the bone wondering, is that true?

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: Would you share with our listeners your experiences regarding your daughter, was it?

speaker: Sue Hurst
words: I went to school some 20 years ago out in Aravada west, and at the time it was very small community that was growing, and there was a place out where kids like to go to picnic, and you know, have parties and all, and have bonfires at night, and just sit and tell ghost stories and stuff, you know, like Molly Hatchet from Red Rocks, you know, all the scary stuff, and you know, being a Girl Scout, you know, all of us in this area were real, you know, love to be out in the country and hike and in all of this, and in 1969 of course, we had the big fire out there, that was the biggest industrial fire, other than the 57 fire, you know, when you think about the cost of one troy ounce of gold per one troy ounce of plutonium, plutonium is eight times the price of gold, so this stuff's expensive, and I'm wondering if this is why the home values go up the closer you get to Rocky Flats, you're paying for the plutonium. But you think about all the dust that settled out by Leyden, which is just just over the rise from Rocky Flats, they had the open pit uranium mine burning, which again will release radioactivity to that area and settle on Leyden Lake. I went out there swimming in the lake many, many times and got pregnant my senior year, and consequently, when I had my daughter, I was living up in Lake Tahoe, and when she was born, she didn't have the sucking reflex action. She couldn't keep her body temperature up, and this really puzzled these doctors at Barton Memorial, because basically it's a resort hospital, they're set up to do ski breaks, you know. And when Ann Margaret fell off the stage, they had to fly her down to LA, you know. It's no joke, that place is a ridiculous excuse for a hospital. It's more like a clinic. So they moved my daughter to another hospital to find out why what happened, because she was, she was a beautiful baby, gorgeous, beautiful eyes, head of brown, dark hair. But when the doctors called me a week later, I was in no shape to travel because I was, I had to have a cesarean section, and I couldn't go with her, otherwise I would have. She did not, she almost didn't survive the trip, she almost expired by the time they got her the hospital, but they told me that their studies showed them that she had a condition known as hydrocephalic...
